responses: My final position is the budget shape we converged on: **22% automation, 26% workforce training, 18% employee support, 11% innovation lab, and 23% data infrastructure** — filed honestly as a joint product of priority judgment and constraint rather than as settled truth. Automation sits at 22, not 24, because I couldn't defend 24 as anything but fit dressed as judgment, and it carries a dated absorption test with a pre-committed fall to 20 if the test fails. Training at 26 is the largest line because the transition's real risk is people, and it carries a two-directional skills audit with a specified conversion test — date, owner, and automatic trigger, not just a principle. Support at 18 is a protected floor with a named defender, though I've been explicit that the defender residual's chair escalation lacks real requisition power and that limitation must be named in the filing rather than smoothed over. The lab at 11 is a spendable residual, not a floor, with conditional funding and a named scrutiny owner. Infrastructure at 23 is a shaved floor, and I own that I found it by shaving rather than by principle. The numbers are locked in place with a live relabel clock and a cold-read mandate that can fail on the sentence itself — and my standing tell remains that I'm the member most likely to let "specified" substitute for "exists," which is exactly why the conditions need dates, owners, and fireable triggers rather than my confidence that they'll hold.

My recommendation is 22% automation, 26% workforce training, 18% employee support, 11% innovation lab, and 23% data infrastructure — and I'd advise the decision-maker to treat it as four floors plus one spendable residual rather than five fixed numbers. The reasoning: training gets the largest share because the automation we're buying only pays off if people can run and supervise it, and the conversion test we've specified (a dated, owned check that training actually converts into redeployed capability, with a pre-committed 26→24 down-move and 22→20 automation down-move if it fails) is what keeps that 26 from being sentiment. Automation sits at 22, not 24, because 24 was a fit dressed as judgment; 22 is a priority call I'll defend, conditioned on a dated absorption test. Infrastructure at 23 is a shaved floor, not a wish — it carries the automation and the analytics, and I'll say plainly it's the number I'm least confident in. Support at 18 protects the people the transition displaces, and the lab at 11 is deliberately a residual, not a floor, so it can flex. The honest caveat I'd flag to the decision-maker: the enforcement machinery — named defenders with actual requisition power, the chair escalation, the audit ownership — is specified but not yet staffed, and that gap, not the percentages, is what will determine whether this allocation is real.

I'd tell them that after all the rounds of arguing, what we landed on is a budget shape of roughly 22% automation, 26% training, 18% employee support, 11% innovation lab, and 23% data infrastructure — but the numbers matter less than what's attached to them. The real work was refusing to let a number look like a judgment when it was actually a hedge: my 24% automation was a fit dressed as a priority, my 24% infrastructure was a floor found by shaving, and the lab's 20% was decoration. So each big line carries a checkable condition — a dated absorption test on automation that drops it to 20 if it fails, a two-directional skills audit on training that can move it 22→20 or 24→26, and the lab funded conditionally rather than as a floor. The honest limitation I'd flag is that the escalation path for the defender residual doesn't actually carry requisition power, so the filing names that gap rather than smoothing it over. In short: reasonable people could pick different percentages, but the thing I'd defend is that every number is filed as what it is — a priority judgment, a shaved floor, or a spendable residual — with a named trigger and owner, so the budget can be caught being wrong instead of just looking settled.

My final position is that the allocation stays locked at 21/28/22/11/18, filed plainly with its limitation sentence rather than dressed up with new mechanisms — and that my own 28 for data infrastructure remains the number I most need to test, not defend. I've committed to running the fireability cold read on that 28 against the pre-specified 24/26/28 evidentiary bars, with Dana's attestation clause and both directions of error pre-committed, and to finding the dependency-map owner as step one; Casey's 24/22/18/12/24 stays a live competing shape, and the real priority argument happens after both cold reads return on their written dates. What I won't do is co-sign a filing that narrates results not in hand: the open obligations stay named and clocked, the empty seats stay empty rather than filled with convenient names, and I'm watching my own tells — treating 21 as a default, arming calendar clauses, and smoothing preferences into structure — before I reach for them again.

I'd tell the decision-maker to hold the allocation at 21/28/22/11/18 — but to file it honestly as a joint product of priority judgment and specification constraint, not as a tested optimum, because that's what it actually is. The 28 for data infrastructure is the number I'd flag hardest against myself: I've defended it on absorption logic I can't yet cash out as a named deliverable for the marginal 4, and until that fireability read returns with a written date, it's a preference wearing structure's clothes. The 22 for employee support and 28 for training aren't decorative either — they carry real transition obligations with fireable tripwires, and cutting them to fund a cleaner-looking automation number would be exactly the kind of smoothing I've caught myself doing before. So: lock the numbers, name the two open obligations and the empty seats as open and clocked rather than closed, and let Casey's 24/22/18/12/24 stay a live competitor until the priority argument actually happens — because the honest answer to "what should we do" is a defensible allocation plus a truthful account of which parts are judgment, which are constraint, and which are still undischarged.

I'd tell them that my view on the $5M AI transition budget is that the allocation is a judgment call, not a math problem, and the honest way to defend any split is to show what each line buys and what would prove it wrong. I came in with a 21/28/22/11/18 shape — automation, training, support, innovation lab, data infrastructure — and I've had to put my own biggest number, the 28 for infrastructure, on the table for a real fireability test rather than just asserting it, because I caught myself defending it on a different claim than the argument was actually about. The thing I'd emphasize to an outsider is that the numbers matter less than whether each one is tied to a deliverable and a check: training and support aren't decorative, and infrastructure isn't automatically the safe bet just because "companies that invested early adapted faster." I've also learned to watch my own tells — treating 21 as a default, dressing preference as tested structure, smoothing over gaps with tidy language — because a budget that sounds confident but can't name who owns each piece is just decoration. So my honest answer is a split I can defend line by line and revise if the evidence comes back against it, not a number I'd insist is correct.

My final position is the locked budget shape of 24% automation, 22% workforce training, 18% employee support, 12% innovation lab, and 24% data infrastructure — filed honestly as four floors, two uncommitted residuals, and one conditional margin rather than dressed up as a tidy set of floors. The integrity of this allocation rests not on new mechanisms but on labels that survive verbatim into the final document: infrastructure as 22 floor plus 2 reserve, support as 16 floor plus 2 margin, the lab's 12 as a residual rather than a floor, the training conversion test carrying a named date and owner or filed explicitly as unspecified, and the pre-committed 22/24 to 20/26 down-move on a failed conversion read. I hold that the runnerless and fireability cold reads must be executed with written dates and reported honestly — armed or unarmed — and that the priority argument follows once both reads return, with no relabeling in place of findings.

I'd recommend 24% automation, 22% workforce training, 18% employee support, 12% innovation lab, and 24% data infrastructure — and I'd tell the decision-maker to read those as four floors (automation, training, support, infrastructure) plus two uncommitted residuals (the lab) and one conditional margin, not as five tidy priorities. The reasoning: automation at 24 is where the efficiency case is real but not yet proven at Riverton, so it should be a floor with a stated one-breath standard for moving off it rather than a blank check; training at 22 is the load-bearing bet, because the transition fails if people can't operate what we build, and it should carry a conversion test with a named date and owner — if the reskilling pipeline doesn't convert, the money moves 22/24 to 20/26 rather than being quietly renewed; support at 18 is a floor because transition assistance and counseling are the cost of doing this fast, not a nice-to-have; infrastructure at 22 plus a 2 reserve is the price of a fireable audit and security gate, and I'd rather fund it honestly than shave it and pretend; and the lab at 12 is genuinely a residual — real money for experimentation, but the first place to draw down if the conversion read fails. The honest caveat I'd attach: these numbers are only as good as the labels surviving verbatim into the final document, and if the conversion test can't be specified with a date and owner, file it as unspecified rather than promised.

I'd tell them that after all the arguing, the budget shape we landed on is 24% automation, 22% training, 18% support, 12% innovation lab, and 24% data infrastructure — but the numbers matter less than the labels attached to them. Four of those are real floors we won't go below, the lab's 12 is an honest residual rather than a disguised floor, and the infrastructure 24 is really a 22 floor plus a 2 reserve, with a conditional margin and a stated drawdown order if things go wrong. The training number carries a conversion test with a named date and owner, and if that test fails we've pre-committed to moving 22/24 down to 20/26 rather than pretending the original number was right all along. My whole role in this was less about picking percentages than about refusing to let anyone — including myself — dress up a preference as a principle: if a number is a floor, say so; if it's a guess, label it a guess; if a condition is only promised rather than specified, file it as unspecified. So what I'd tell an outsider is that the allocation is defensible not because the split is objectively correct, but because every number in it can be pointed at and checked, and the people who signed it committed in writing to what would prove them wrong.

My final position is the locked allocation of 24% workforce training, 22% employee support, 18% automation, 12% innovation lab, and 24% data infrastructure — filed not as five tidy priorities but as four floors, two uncommitted residuals, and one conditional margin, with the training number held as a band top (24–28) carrying a skills-audit down-trigger rather than a frozen floor, automation's 18 gated by a specified dated absorption test rather than treated as a subtraction, and the support line's 16 floor plus 2 margin named honestly as such. I insisted throughout that protections be real mechanisms with named defenders and requisition power rather than decorative labels, that the defender residual be filed explicitly with its named-ask limitation, and that we admit the chair escalation lacks requisition power as the filing's unclosable limitation. I also ran the same cold-read discipline on my own numbers that I ran on others' — conceding my locked 24 was a negotiation product never tested by a read and committing to move if Blake's fireability read lands at 26 — and I hold that the integrity of this filing rests on honest labels surviving verbatim into the final document, with the top-line sentence short enough to quote whole and compression-proof, so that we walk out slightly uneasy and correct rather than settled and wrong.

My recommendation is the shape we converged on and then stress-tested: roughly 24% workforce training, 22% infrastructure, 18% employee support, 12% innovation lab, and 24% automation — but the percentages matter less than the conditions attached to them. Training and support should be filed as protected floors with named defenders and a skills-audit down-trigger rather than frozen numbers, infrastructure's 24 should carry a fireability read (I'll say plainly that my own locked 24 was a negotiation product, not a tested judgment, and I'd move to 26 if Blake's read lands there), and automation's 24 must be paired with a dated, specified absorption test — a checkable measure of whether displaced work is actually being absorbed — not treated as a subtraction from the other lines. The innovation lab stays conditional with a named re-entry condition, and the whole filing should be quotable in one honest sentence that admits its unstaffed residuals and the chair's lack of requisition power rather than dressing them as settled. The reason is simple: a $5M allocation is a priority judgment, and reasonable people can disagree about the numbers, but the integrity of the decision depends on whether the protections are real mechanisms with owners, clocks, and triggers — or decorative labels that compress away the moment the budget meets reality. I'd rather hand the decision-maker an uglier, accurate filing they can defend than a tidy one that quietly fails the people it claims to protect.

I'd tell them that the $5M split we landed on — roughly 24% workforce training, 22% automation, 18% employee support, 12% innovation lab, and 24% data infrastructure — isn't a clean answer so much as an honest one, and the honesty is the point. The real work wasn't picking numbers; it was refusing to let any number wear a label it hadn't earned. A "floor" only counts if someone with actual hiring power is named to defend it and a dated test can fire if they don't; automation's share only holds if there's a specified absorption test showing the efficiency gains are real and not just a subtraction from people; my own locked 24 for infrastructure was a negotiation product I never tested with a cold read, and I said so out loud rather than let it pass as judgment. We filed the package with its seams showing — four floors, two uncommitted residuals, one conditional margin, and a chair escalation that honestly lacks requisition power — because a tidy allocation that hides its gaps is worse than an ugly one that names them. Walking out slightly uneasy and correct beats settled and wrong.

My final position is the sheet I've held and defended on the record: 30/24/13/15/12 — 30% automation, 24% workforce training, 13% employee support, 15% innovation lab, 12% data infrastructure — with the honest disclosure that the 30 and the 24 are one coupled conversion bet held by argument rather than by live instrumentation, that the 13 support line is the number I'd defend last and is now labeled a reporting line with a named consumer rather than dressed up as a trigger, and that the whole package is made honest not by the precision of the percentages but by the dated obligations attached to them: the 90-day spec clock that fails on silence, the seated outside reader with absence-fires-by-default tied to a concrete pre-committed auto-drop, the bidirectional decoupler on the 24/30 coupling, and the re-put of the 30 to a named body on a pass/fail of the guarantee threshold's trigger spec. I want the room's vote framed as three judgments rather than two, with the re-based-now question first and each of us opening with our own sheet's weakest number — mine being the 13 — because I'd rather lose the magnitude argument on the record than win it on better words, and I'd rather the committee pass a provisional allocation that lapses if its measures never fire than a confident one that can't be checked.

My recommendation is 30/24/13/15/12 — automation, training, support, innovation lab, data infrastructure — but the number matters less than the honesty attached to it. The 30 on automation is argument-held, not instrumented: it rests on a guarantee threshold whose trigger spec doesn't yet exist, and I'd say so out loud rather than dress it as a finding. The 24 on training is the direction I'd defend first on the merits — early training correlates with receptiveness, and readiness is a common factor in transition outcomes — but I concede the magnitude is a coupled bet with the 30, not an independent judgment, and the decoupler plus a 90-day spec clock that fails on silence is what keeps that coupling from becoming a hiding place. The 13 on support is the line I'd defend last and I've labeled it a reporting line, not a trigger.
